question: After running hdfs namenode -format to reformat and starting the cluster, the DataNode fails to start and the log reports Incompatible clusterIDs. What should I do?
context: Each time namenode -format is run, a new VERSION file is generated under the NameNode's dfs.namenode.name.dir with a new clusterID; the DataNode's dfs.datanode.data.dir, however, still keeps the old clusterID from the previous format. When the clusterIDs of the NameNode and DataNode do not match, the DataNode registration is rejected and Incompatible clusterIDs is thrown.
ground_truth: Stop the cluster (stop-dfs.sh). Either of the following: 1) Copy the clusterID value from the NameNode's dfs/name/current/VERSION file and overwrite the clusterID field in each DataNode's dfs/data/current/VERSION file, then save and restart; 2) after confirming there is no important data, delete all contents under each DataNode's dfs/data directory and restart, letting the DataNode re-register with the NameNode. Note: do not run namenode -format again.

question: After start-dfs.sh, jps shows no DataNode, and the log says the datanode clusterID does not match the namenode clusterID. How do I fix this?
context: The HDFS NameNode and DataNode each record the clusterID in their own local storage directory's current/VERSION file; the two must match exactly, otherwise the DataNode exits at startup because of a clusterID mismatch. The location of this VERSION file differs across Hadoop versions, so look it up according to the dfs.namenode.name.dir / dfs.datanode.data.dir configuration.
ground_truth: First use grep -r clusterID under the dfs data directories to locate the NameNode and DataNode VERSION files; change the clusterID in the NameNode VERSION to match the DataNode's (or vice versa, so both take the same value); after synchronizing the change, run stop-dfs.sh && start-dfs.sh on all nodes, then use jps to confirm the DataNode process exists.

question: After formatting HDFS for the first time and using it for a while, I ran hdfs namenode -format again, and now the DataNode cannot start. What is the cause?
context: Running namenode -format again clears the NameNode metadata directory and generates a new namespaceID/clusterID, but it does not clear the old version information under the DataNode data directory. This results in Incompatible namespaceIDs / clusterID: the NameNode namespaceID and datanode namespaceID do not match, and the DataNode refuses to serve.
ground_truth: The correct procedure is: stop the cluster, delete all data under dfs.data.dir (default ${hadoop.tmp.dir}/dfs/data) on every DataNode node, as well as the contents of the NameNode's dfs.name.dir, then run hdfs namenode -format once more and start the cluster. Always back up metadata before formatting in production; formatting causes existing HDFS data to be lost.

question: HDFS stays in safe mode and hdfs dfs -put cannot write, reporting The node is in safe mode. How do I get out?
context: After the NameNode starts it enters Safemode (read-only mode), waiting for DataNodes to report their blocks; it does not leave automatically while the percentage of reported blocks is below the threshold dfs.namenode.safemode.threshold.pct (default 0.999). Under Safemode, HDFS does not allow modifying the filesystem or blocks.
ground_truth: First run hdfs dfsadmin -report to confirm all DataNodes are online and no blocks are lost; if everything looks normal, run hdfs dfsadmin -safemode leave as the hdfs superuser to force leaving; if blocks are missing and the threshold cannot be met, use hdfs fsck / to check for corrupt blocks and repair them first, and do not blindly force leave or you may lose data. If needed, lower dfs.namenode.safemode.threshold.pct.

question: After Hadoop starts, the NameNode stays stuck in safe mode and dfsadmin -safemode leave has no effect. What could be the cause?
context: The NameNode stays in safe mode usually because: the reported block percentage is below the default threshold 0.999f, not all DataNodes are online, blocks have been lost due to operations, or DataNodes are reporting blocks slowly. The NameNode leaves safe mode automatically only once the block reporting rate reaches the threshold.
ground_truth: First run hdfs dfsadmin -report to confirm all DataNode processes are running; if any DataNode is down, restore it first; use hdfs fsck / to check for missing/corrupt blocks; once block health is confirmed, run hdfs dfsadmin -safemode leave; if DataNodes are reporting slowly, wait or raise dfs.namenode.safemode.extension.

question: Running hdfs dfsadmin -safemode leave reports Access denied: Superuser privilege is required. What should I do?
context: The HDFS superuser is the OS user that started the NameNode process itself; the permission check never fails for the superuser. An ordinary OS user (including root) is not the same as the HDFS superuser. Running dfsadmin administrative commands such as safemode/balancer as a non-hdfs user reports superuser privilege is required.
ground_truth: Switch to the OS user that started the NameNode (usually hdfs) and run it again: sudo -u hdfs hdfs dfsadmin -safemode leave; on a secure cluster, first run kinit to obtain a ticket for the hdfs user or a supergroup user, then run it. Do not run administrative commands directly as root.

question: The Hadoop startup log keeps printing WARN util.NativeCodeLoader: Unable to load native-hadoop library for your platform. Is this serious, and how do I fix it?
context: The native-hadoop library is a C-written local library for compression (zlib/gzip) and encryption; it only supports *nix platforms (not Cygwin or Mac OS X). The binary distribution ships a .so compiled for a specific platform; when loading fails on a mismatched OS/architecture (e.g. Windows, 32/64-bit mismatch, or wrong glibc version), it only logs a warning, and HDFS can still run using the Java fallback codecs, with slightly lower performance.
ground_truth: This warning does not affect basic functionality; to enable native compression/performance, install the zlib development package for the corresponding platform and compile the native library from source, or use a prebuilt distribution matching your OS; confirm io.native.lib.available is true in hdfs-site/core-site, and use hadoop checknative -a to check the status of the native libraries. On Windows this warning can be ignored.

question: While running a MapReduce job the log shows NativeCodeLoader: Unable to load native-hadoop library. How do I confirm whether the native library actually loaded successfully?
context: The bin/hadoop script specifies the native library path via -Djava.library.path; at runtime, if the log shows NativeCodeLoader - Loaded the native-hadoop library, it loaded successfully, whereas Unable to load native-hadoop library means it fell back to the Java implementation.
ground_truth: Use the command hadoop checknative -a to check whether native libraries such as zlib and openssl are correctly recognized; confirm that the .so architecture under $HADOOP_HOME/lib/native matches the JVM (a 64-bit JVM pairs with 64-bit native); if needed, export JAVA_LIBRARY_PATH=$HADOOP_HOME/lib/native in hadoop-env.sh.

question: Running a job on Hadoop 2.7 reports java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: Unsupported major.minor version 52.0. What does this mean?
context: major.minor 52.0 corresponds to a class file compiled for Java 8; this error means the class was compiled with a higher JDK version, but the JVM running it is older (e.g. Java 7). Hadoop 2.x officially requires Java 7/8, and all jars in Hadoop 3.x are compiled targeting Java 8, so starting with Java 7 inevitably raises the 52.0 error.
ground_truth: Check the running JVM with java -version; upgrade the runtime JDK to match the compile version (Hadoop 2.7 recommends Java 7/8, Hadoop 3.x requires Java 8 or higher), export JAVA_HOME in hadoop-env.sh to point to the higher JDK, restart the cluster, then run the job again.

question: What is the minimum required Java version for Hadoop 3.0? Can I still use Java 7?
context: Starting from Hadoop 3.0.0, the minimum required Java version was raised from Java 7 to Java 8, and all Hadoop jars are compiled targeting the Java 8 runtime; users still on Java 7 or below must upgrade to Java 8.
ground_truth: Upgrade the JDK to Java 8 (Hadoop 3.3.x recommends Java 8 or Java 11), change JAVA_HOME in /etc/profile and hadoop-env.sh, run java -version to confirm, then restart the Hadoop cluster.

question: Can Hadoop 3.3.4 run directly on Java 11?
context: Hadoop 3.3.4 has completed Java 11 runtime support (Java 11 runtime support is completed); starting from Hadoop 3.3.0 it supports TLS 1.3 on Java 11 (11.0.3 and above). Starting from Hadoop 3.5.0 the server side requires Java 17, while the client supports Java 17/21.
ground_truth: Hadoop 3.3.x can run on Java 8 or Java 11 in production (3.3.5+ can experimentally use Java 17); Hadoop 3.4.x recommends Java 11 or Java 17; Hadoop 3.5.x requires Java 17 on the server side. Set JAVA_HOME according to the chosen version and avoid mixing them.

question: Hadoop 3.4.1 shows Protobuf-related compatibility issues on some JDK8 builds. How should I handle this?
context: The Hadoop 3.4.1 release notes state that this version has Protobuf compatibility issues with certain JDK8 versions, and recommend upgrading to a higher JDK (>JDK8) in production; future 3.4.x releases will resolve it by upgrading the Protobuf in hadoop-thirdparty, and will drop support for JDK8.
ground_truth: Upgrade the JDK to Java 11 or higher; if you must stay on JDK8, upgrade to a fixed minor version within 3.4.x, or temporarily reduce the affected Protobuf usage; do not use JDK8 long-term on 3.4.1.

question: Writing a file to HDFS reports File could only be replicated to 0 nodes instead of minReplication (=1). How do I troubleshoot?
context: This exception means the NameNode cannot find a DataNode to place the block on: possibly the DataNode has not finished registering with the NameNode, all DataNodes are down, a disk is full and treated as a bad volume, or the firewall/network is unreachable. If the X in 'There are X datanode(s) running' in the error is 0, the reporting link from DataNode to NameNode has a problem.
ground_truth: First run hdfs dfsadmin -report to see the number of online DataNodes; if it is 0, check the DataNode process, the fs.defaultFS address in core-site.xml, connectivity to ports 9000/8020, and the firewall; if DataNodes are up but a disk is full, clear the disk holding dfs.data.dir; right after startup, wait for DataNode registration to complete before writing.

question: After a Docker container restart I reformatted HDFS, and uploading a file reports could only be replicated to 0 nodes. What should I do?
context: Reformatting HDFS makes the NameNode generate a new version number/clusterID, while the DataNode data directory still holds the old version; the version mismatch causes the DataNode to be excluded even though it is running, so the client cannot replicate the file to any node.
ground_truth: Change the clusterID in the DataNode's dfs/data/current/VERSION file to match the NameNode's dfs/name/current/VERSION, and restart the cluster; do not run namenode -format again. In container scenarios it is better to use a fixed data volume and avoid repeated formatting.

question: Under single-node pseudo-distributed mode dfs.replication defaults to 3, but there is only one DataNode. What happens when I write a file?
context: dfs.replication defaults to 3 (across Hadoop versions), meaning each block is kept in 3 replicas; a single-node pseudo-distributed cluster has only 1 DataNode and cannot satisfy 3 replicas, so the official single-node install docs require explicitly setting dfs.replication to 1.
ground_truth: Add the following to etc/hadoop/hdfs-site.xml: <property><name>dfs.replication</name><value>1</value></property>, then restart HDFS. For existing files you can adjust the replica count individually with hdfs dfs -setrep -w 1 /path.

question: The DataNode log reports Retrying connect to server: master/192.168.x.x:9000 failed on connection exception: Connection refused. What is going on?
context: 9000 (or 8020 in 3.x) is the NameNode RPC address, specified by fs.defaultFS in core-site.xml. Connection refused means the NameNode process is not running, the bound address/port is misconfigured, or a firewall is blocking it; usually it is because the NameNode is not up yet or the hostname/IP in core-site.xml is wrong.
ground_truth: On the NameNode host, use jps to confirm the NameNode process exists; use netstat -tnlp | grep 9000 to confirm the port is listening; check whether the hostname in fs.defaultFS in core-site.xml can be resolved by the DataNode (/etc/hosts); turn off the firewall or open ports 9000/8020.

question: Starting Hive reports Call From master/192.168.x.x to master:9000 failed on connection exception: Connection refused. How do I fix it?
context: This connection refusal means there is no service listening on the NameNode RPC port 9000 that the client (Hive) is reaching: either the Hadoop cluster is not started, or fs.defaultFS in core-site.xml is misconfigured (wrong hostname/port), or the NameNode was never formatted and failed to start.
ground_truth: First run start-dfs.sh on the NameNode node and use jps to confirm both NameNode and DataNode are present; check that the fs.defaultFS value in core-site.xml matches the actual NameNode host; for first-time use, run hdfs namenode -format first; confirm port 9000 is not occupied by another program.

question: Starting the NameNode reports java.net.BindException: Address already in use, i.e. the port is occupied. What should I do?
context: BindException: Address already in use means the RPC port (9000/8020) or HTTP port (9870) the NameNode wants to bind is already taken by another process; this commonly happens when the previous process was killed with kill -9 and the port was not released, or the port is occupied by another program.
ground_truth: Use netstat -tnlp | grep -E '9000|9870|8020' (or lsof -i:9000) to find the PID holding the port, kill it, then start the NameNode; if the port is in TIME_WAIT due to an abnormal previous exit, wait a moment or shorten the TCP TIME_WAIT duration; you can also change the corresponding port in core-site/hdfs-site.

question: Hadoop 3.1.3 fails to start and the NameNode log shows the port is in use. What are the common troubleshooting steps?
context: Hadoop's daemon ports are fixed: NameNode RPC 8020, NameNode HTTP 9870, DataNode 9866/9864, ResourceManager 8088, NodeManager 8042, etc. A port being occupied causes the corresponding daemon to exit immediately after starting, so check the logs directory for the specific port.
ground_truth: Look at $HADOOP_HOME/logs/hadoop-*-namenode-*.log to determine the occupied port; use netstat -anp | grep <port> to find the occupying process; kill the leftover java process or change the configured port; ensure stop-dfs.sh / stop-yarn.sh run cleanly before starting again.

question: The ResourceManager will not start and the log reports Caused by: java.net.BindException: Port in use: x.x.x.x:8088. What is the cause?
context: 8088 is the ResourceManager Web UI port. BindException is often due to the cluster node IP changing while yarn-site.xml still has the old IP in yarn.resourcemanager.hostname / address, or port 8088 being occupied by a leftover process.
ground_truth: Check the node's current IP (hostname -I / ifconfig), and update yarn.resourcemanager.address and yarn.resourcemanager.webapp.address in yarn-site.xml to the correct hostname/IP; use netstat to confirm 8088 is free; restart the ResourceManager.

question: The DataNode log reports Too many open files, and while running MapReduce all datanodes are bad. How do I tune this?
context: The Linux default per-process open file limit (ulimit -n) is usually 1024; Hadoop's DataNode/NodeManager needs to hold a large number of file handles at once (blocks, shuffle outputs), and when it falls short it throws Too many open files and is judged a bad volume/bad node.
ground_truth: Run ulimit -n to see the current value; in /etc/security/limits.conf (or /etc/security/limits.d/90-nofile.conf) set nofile to 65536 or higher for the hdfs/yarn users (production recommends 64000~655360), and raise nproc as well; re-login or restart the node, then verify with ulimit -n.

question: Starting the DataNode on a secure cluster reports Too many open files. What ulimit configuration does the official guide recommend?
context: The Cloudera/HDP security guide recommends: when the open-file count is too low at DataNode startup, it throws Too Many Open Files; the recommended nofile (max open files) is 32768 and nproc (max processes) is 65536.
ground_truth: As root, add to /etc/security/limits.conf: hdfs - nofile 32768 and hdfs - nproc 65536 (replace with the actual OS user), restart the DataNode, then verify with sudo -u hdfs ulimit -a.

question: The DataNode startup is rejected by the NameNode, reporting Datanode denied communication with namenode because hostname cannot be resolved. What should I do?
context: Since Hadoop 2, the NameNode enables dfs.namenode.datanode.registration.ip-hostname-check=true by default, which does a reverse DNS lookup on the connecting DataNode address; if the hostname cannot be resolved, it throws DisallowedDatanodeException and rejects the registration.
ground_truth: The correct approach is to configure /etc/hosts or internal DNS on all nodes so that each node's IP reverse-resolves to a hostname and the hostname forward-resolves to an IP. As a temporary workaround, set dfs.namenode.datanode.registration.ip-hostname-check=false in hdfs-site.xml (not recommended in production, as it allows malicious registration when DNS fails).

question: Running Hadoop in a Docker / no-DNS environment, the NameNode log reports DisallowedDatanodeException. How do I handle this?
context: Without DNS, or with dynamically changing container IPs, the NameNode cannot reverse-resolve the DataNode hostname, leading to Datanode denied communication with namenode. The official multihoming docs recommend explicitly disabling hostname verification in such environments, or letting DataNodes do the DNS resolution themselves.
ground_truth: Add to hdfs-site.xml: <property><name>dfs.namenode.datanode.registration.ip-hostname-check</name><value>false</value></property>; also configure /etc/hosts to fix the hostname mappings; restart HDFS and confirm the DataNode count in the NameNode Web UI.

question: In a cross-network / multi-NIC environment, DataNodes cannot connect to each other and the IP the NameNode resolves is unreachable. How do I handle this?
context: In rare cases the IP the NameNode resolves for a DataNode is unreachable from other DataNodes (multihomed network). The official docs provide the dfs.datanode.use.datanode.hostname parameter to force DataNodes to use the hostname rather than the IP when connecting between nodes.
ground_truth: Set in hdfs-site.xml: <property><name>dfs.datanode.use.datanode.hostname</name><value>true</value></property>, and ensure all node hostnames resolve to each other; bind the server-side address to 0.0.0.0 (INADDR_ANY) to listen on all NICs.

question: Is the Hadoop 3.x NameNode HTTP port different from 2.x? I can no longer open the Web UI on 50070.
context: Hadoop 3.x changed the NameNode HTTP port from 50070 in 2.x to 9870, and the HTTPS port from 50470 to 9871; DataNode ports were adjusted accordingly (9866/9864). Using the 2.x habit of accessing 50070 gives connection refused.
ground_truth: On Hadoop 3.x access the NameNode Web UI at http://nn-host:9870; if you customized the port, look up dfs.namenode.http-address in hdfs-site.xml; open port 9870 in the firewall.

question: A YARN job's container gets killed mid-run, and the log reports Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits. What should I do?
context: The NodeManager monitors a container's physical/virtual memory and kills the container when it exceeds the allocated limit (the exit code corresponds to KILLED_EXCEEDED_PMEM for physical memory exceeded / KILLED_EXCEEDED_VMEM for virtual memory exceeded). Common causes are mapreduce.map.memory.mb / mapreduce.reduce.memory.mb or Spark executor memory set too low, with JVM off-heap memory counted in.
ground_truth: Raise mapreduce.map.memory.mb, mapreduce.reduce.memory.mb and the corresponding mapreduce.map.java.opts heap size in mapred-site.xml; also check whether yarn.nodemanager.pmem-check-enabled is too strict; in the Spark case raise spark.executor.memoryOverhead. Look at the process tree at kill time in the NM log to determine whether it was PMEM or VMEM.

question: A YARN container is killed with exit code 137. How do I tell whether it was an OOM or a manual kill?
context: Exit code 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL); it may be YARN killing it for exceeding physical/virtual memory, or the system OOM killer. Under YARN cgroups strict memory control mode, containers over the limit are killed directly; distinguish the two by combining NodeManager logs and system logs.
ground_truth: Check the NodeManager log to confirm whether it was exceeding physical/virtual memory; check dmesg / /var/log/messages for Linux OOM killer records; if it was a YARN memory limit, raise the container memory; if it was a system OOM, add physical memory to the node or reduce concurrent containers.

question: A Spark on YARN job frequently reports Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits. How do I tune the parameters?
context: This error means the application requested insufficient memory: at startup the JVM's actual usage (including off-heap) exceeds the container memory allocated by YARN, and the NodeManager terminates the container; Spark is especially prone to this because of its heavy off-heap memory use.
ground_truth: In the Spark configuration raise spark.driver.memoryOverhead and spark.executor.memoryOverhead (e.g. from 384 to 1g+), and correspondingly adjust yarn.nodemanager.resource.memory-mb and the scheduler minimum allocation granularity in yarn-site.xml; restart the Spark job and observe.

question: What parameters determine the memory upper limit of a MapReduce map/reduce container?
context: YARN allocates a container for each map/reduce task, and the memory upper limit is determined by mapreduce.map.memory.mb / mapreduce.reduce.memory.mb; a task that actually uses more than this limit is killed. It must also be coordinated with yarn.scheduler.minimum-allocation-mb / maximum-allocation-mb.
ground_truth: Set mapreduce.map.memory.mb=4096 and mapreduce.reduce.memory.mb=8192 in mapred-site.xml (depending on cluster size), and set the corresponding JVM heap mapreduce.map.java.opts=-Xmx3072m, with the reduce heap at about 75-80% of the container; ensure yarn.nodemanager.resource.memory-mb exceeds the per-container requirement.

question: A submitted YARN job stays at ACCEPTED: waiting for AM container to be allocated. What should I do?
context: This state means the ResourceManager accepted the application but has no available resources to start the AM container: common causes are the queue being at capacity (limited by the Capacity Scheduler's capacity/maximum-am-resource-percent), all NodeManagers being offline, or yarn.nodemanager.resource.memory-mb being set too low.
ground_truth: Check the ResourceManager log and ResourceManager Web UI (8088) to see available nodes and queue resources; confirm all NodeManagers are online (yarn node -list); raise the queue's max-am-resource-percent or increase NodeManager resource configuration; submit the job to an idle queue.

question: On a secure cluster the NodeManager startup reports container-executor: java.io.IOException: error=13, Permission denied. How do I fix it?
context: container-executor is the local binary that starts/destroys containers under a secure YARN cluster; it must be setuid root with permissions 6050 and owned by root:yarn. A permission mismatch causes the NodeManager to fail to bootstrap the container subsystem and fail to start.
ground_truth: Locate $HADOOP_HOME/bin/container-executor and run chown root:yarn container-executor && chmod 6050 container-executor; check the conf/container-executor.cfg configuration; restart the NodeManager.

question: After a NodeManager restart the task is stuck at ACCEPTED, and the log reports LevelDB NativeDB$DBException. What should I do?
context: The NodeManager's state store is based on LevelDB; an abnormal exit or power loss can corrupt the state DB, so the NodeManager cannot register with the ResourceManager and all applications stay permanently stuck at ACCEPTED.
ground_truth: Stop the NodeManager; delete its local state directory (the state-store directory, separate from the default yarn.nodemanager.node-logs-dir, usually under $HADOOP_YARN_HOME/data/nm-state or the configured path); restart the NodeManager so it re-registers with the RM. Note: back up before deleting.

question: Running Hadoop locally on Windows reports java.io.IOException: Could not locate executable null\bin\winutils.exe. How do I fix it?
context: On Windows, Hadoop relies on winutils.exe (and hadoop.dll) to perform POSIX operations such as permissions/symlinks; the program locates $HADOOP_HOME/bin/winutils.exe via the system property hadoop.home.dir (i.e. HADOOP_HOME). When HADOOP_HOME is not set, the path becomes null\bin\winutils.exe.
ground_truth: Set the system environment variable HADOOP_HOME to point to the Hadoop unzip directory, and add %HADOOP_HOME%\bin to PATH; download winutils.exe and hadoop.dll matching your Hadoop version and place them under %HADOOP_HOME%\bin; restart the IDE/command line and run again.

question: On Windows 7 starting start-dfs.cmd reports Failed to locate the winutils binary in the hadoop binary path. How do I handle it?
context: The Hadoop Shell class uses getWinUtilsPath() to look up winutils.exe under HADOOP_HOME/bin; Windows has no native POSIX executable, and missing winutils.exe directly throws this exception.
ground_truth: Configure the user environment variable HADOOP_HOME to the winutils unzip directory, append %HADOOP_HOME%\bin to Path; put the matching winutils.exe into that bin directory; reopen the command line and run echo %HADOOP_HOME% to verify.

question: Starting HDFS on Windows reports Could not locate Hadoop executable: E:\...\bin\winutils.exe, but the path is correct. Why does it still error?
context: A correct path still erroring is usually because the winutils.exe version does not match the Hadoop version (wrong bitness, or hadoop.dll is missing), or it was not run with administrator privileges, causing hadoop.dll to fail to load.
ground_truth: Download the winutils distribution matching the Hadoop major version (including winutils.exe and hadoop.dll) and place it in the bin directory; run the command prompt as administrator; in the IDE explicitly set it with System.setProperty("hadoop.home.dir", "E:/hadoop").

question: When start-dfs.sh starts, it keeps prompting for the ssh localhost password and the script hangs. How do I configure passwordless SSH?
context: Hadoop's startup scripts remotely launch daemons on each worker node over SSH, and must be able to SSH passwordless to localhost and all workers as the current user; without passwordless config the script hangs at the password prompt.
ground_truth: Run ssh-keygen -t rsa -P '' -f ~/.ssh/id_rsa (pressing enter at every prompt), then cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys; test that ssh localhost asks for no password; for multi-node clusters use ssh-copy-id to distribute the public key to all workers.

question: Even after configuring passwordless SSH it still reports Permission denied (publickey,password,keyboard-interactive). How do I troubleshoot?
context: Common causes: the ~/.ssh directory permissions are too loose (should be 700), authorized_keys permissions are too loose (should be 600), the .ssh owner is not the current user, or sshd config disables public key authentication.
ground_truth: Run chmod 700 ~/.ssh && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && chown -R $USER:$USER ~/.ssh; confirm PubkeyAuthentication yes and AuthorizedKeysFile .ssh/authorized_keys in /etc/ssh/sshd_config; systemctl restart sshd; use ssh -v localhost to view the detailed handshake and locate the issue.

question: A MapReduce job reports Shuffle failed: Too many fetch-failures in the reduce phase. How do I handle it?
context: The reduce task pulls data over HTTP from the map output nodes; mapreduce.reduce.shuffle.maxfetchfailures defaults to 10: when the fetch failure count for a given map output exceeds this threshold, the task is judged failed. Common causes are the NodeManager running the map being down, the local disk being full, the shuffle port being blocked by a firewall, or inconsistent DNS resolution between nodes.
ground_truth: Check network connectivity and the firewall between map and reduce nodes; confirm the NodeManager local disk is not full and the shuffle handler (mapreduce.shuffle.port) is reachable; raise mapreduce.reduce.shuffle.maxfetchfailures in mapred-site.xml; check whether /etc/hosts hostname resolution is consistent.

question: Running a step on EMR reports Too many fetch-failures / Error reading task output. What is the cause?
context: This error means the current task depends on another task's output (usually a map output), but that output is unavailable: while the reduce waits for the map output, the node running the map fails, the output files are cleaned up, or the shuffle service is unreachable.
ground_truth: Look at the failed task attempt logs to locate which map output failed to fetch; check whether the corresponding NodeManager is healthy and whether there is shuffle residue on the local disk; confirm the map task was not killed by YARN for memory; if needed, raise the reduce fetch retries and rerun the failed step.

question: HDFS capacity usage reached 100% and the upper-layer HBase/Spark is unavailable, but the local disk is only 85% used. Why?
context: HDFS free space is determined jointly by the DataNode disk free space and dfs.datanode.du.reserved (reserved space); when each DataNode's disk usage reaches the dfs.datanode.fsdataset.volume.choosing.percentage threshold, or free space drops below the reserved value, that DataNode stops accepting new blocks and the cluster as a whole becomes read-only/unwritable.
ground_truth: Use hdfs dfsadmin -report to see each DataNode's free and reserved space; clean up old HDFS data (hdfs dfs -rm -r <old directory>) or add disks/nodes; if needed, lower dfs.datanode.du.reserved; then run hdfs balancer to balance data distribution.

question: hdfs dfsadmin -report shows dfs used 100% and a DataNode volume has failed. How do I troubleshoot?
context: When a DataNode's data disk becomes unavailable (full, bad disk, or wrong permissions) it is marked as a failed volume; once all disks are unavailable the DataNode goes offline, cluster free space drops sharply, and report shows used 100%.
ground_truth: Run hdfs dfsadmin -report to find the failed DataNode; log into that node and check df -h for each disk under dfs.data.dir, and dmesg for disk errors; clean the bad disk or replace it, and remove the failed disk from dfs.datanode.data.dir; restart the DataNode; run hdfs balancer to rebalance.

question: On a single DataNode machine the data across multiple disks is unevenly distributed. How do I balance the disks within the same node?
context: The HDFS Balancer only balances data between cluster nodes; the data distribution among multiple disks inside the same DataNode is handled by Diskbalancer, because heavy writes/deletes or disk swaps can cause uneven distribution across disks.
ground_truth: Use the diskbalancer command: hdfs diskbalancer -query <datanode> to view the plan, and hdfs diskbalancer -execute to perform the inter-disk migration; distinguish it from the cluster-level balancer (hdfs balancer).

question: A YARN NodeManager is marked unhealthy because local disk usage exceeded the threshold (default 90%), and tasks cannot be scheduled. What should I do?
context: yarn.nodemanager.disk-health-checker.max-disk-utilization-per-disk-percentage defaults to 90%: once a NodeManager's local disks (including logs, shuffle, and container directories) exceed this threshold, the RM marks it unhealthy and stops assigning tasks.
ground_truth: Clean up logs and YARN container residue on the NodeManager local disk (yarn.nodemanager.local-dirs, log-dirs); or temporarily raise yarn.nodemanager.disk-health-checker.max-disk-utilization-per-disk-percentage; restart the NodeManager and confirm health with yarn node -list -showDetails.

question: I want to rolling-upgrade a Hadoop 2.x cluster to 3.x without downtime. Is this officially supported, and what are the pitfalls?
context: HDFS rolling upgrade is only supported from Hadoop 2.4.0 onward, and rolling upgrades require the cluster to be deployed with HA; Server-Server compatibility guarantees that mixed versions within the same major version are allowed to support rolling upgrade. Cross-major upgrades (2.x to 3.x) cannot be done in one rolling step directly, and Hadoop 3 after HDFS-13541 rejects certain RPCs from Hadoop 2.
ground_truth: The official recommendation: if you want to rolling-upgrade from Hadoop 2 to a new Hadoop 3 that includes HDFS-13541, do it in two steps first—upgrade to an early Hadoop 3 without that change, then upgrade to the target version; disable new features before upgrading and re-enable them afterward; always back up metadata first.

question: Is Hadoop compatible across minor versions (e.g. upgrading 2.1.0 to 2.2.0, upgrading HDFS but not MapReduce)?
context: The official compatibility contract: Client-Server compatibility must be guaranteed, and upgrading one component alone without upgrading the others is allowed (for example upgrading HDFS from 2.1.0 to 2.2.0 without upgrading MapReduce); Server-Server compatibility guarantees that mixed versions within the cluster are allowed to support rolling upgrades.
ground_truth: Minor upgrades within the same major version can upgrade HDFS/YARN/MapReduce separately without breaking interoperation; across major versions (1.x to 2.x, 2.x to 3.x) follow the official migration docs, and the MapReduce 1.x API is kept as binary-compatible as possible on 2.x/3.x.

question: Running a Sqoop job reports Error: Could not find or load main class org.apache.hadoop.mapreduce.v2.app.MRAppMaster. How do I fix it?
context: This error means the MapReduce job has an incomplete classpath when starting MRAppMaster on the NodeManager; it commonly occurs when mixing Hadoop 3.x with an old Sqoop (1.4.7), or when mapreduce.application.classpath is missing, so the jars under share/hadoop/mapreduce are not added to the container classpath.
ground_truth: Run hadoop classpath to confirm the output includes $HADOOP_HOME/share/hadoop/mapreduce/*; check that mapreduce.application.classpath is correct in mapred-site.xml; upgrade Sqoop to a version compatible with Hadoop 3 (e.g. 1.9.x), or complete HADOOP_MAPRED_HOME in the YARN container environment variables.

question: Running a Hadoop program in a local Eclipse/IDE reports Could not find or load main class. How do I configure HADOOP_CLASSPATH?
context: The official MapReduce tutorial requires exporting HADOOP_CLASSPATH=${JAVA_HOME}/lib/tools.jar when compiling user code, so that the hadoop jar command adds the user classes together with Hadoop dependencies to the classpath; without setting it, running directly reports the main class cannot be found.
ground_truth: Set in ~/.bashrc or the IDE run configuration: HADOOP_CLASSPATH=$HADOOP_HOME/share/hadoop/common/*:$HADOOP_HOME/share/hadoop/mapreduce/*:$HADOOP_HOME/share/hadoop/hdfs/*:$HADOOP_HOME/share/hadoop/yarn/*; submit with hadoop jar your.jar com.example.WordCount in out.

question: A Hadoop program reading/writing S3 reports ClassNotFoundException / AWS SDK version conflict. How do I handle it?
context: The S3A client requires the exact same version of the AWS SDK jar that Hadoop was compiled with to work correctly; having multiple AWS SDK versions on the classpath causes errors due to inconsistent class signatures. The safe practice is to use the AWS SDK version that matches the Hadoop build.
ground_truth: Align the versions of hadoop-aws and aws-java-sdk-bundle to the version specified in the Hadoop release notes; do not put AWS SDK jars from other sources on the cluster classpath; use hadoop classpath to check for conflicts and remove duplicate jars if needed.

question: I want to use TLS 1.3 with Hadoop 3.3.0. What are the requirements on the Java version?
context: Hadoop 3.3.0 supports TLS 1.3, but this capability is only available on the Java 11 runtime (11.0.3 and above), and does not include cloud connectors. To enable it you must configure hadoop.ssl.enabled.protocols in core-site.xml.
ground_truth: Run Hadoop 3.3.0+ with Java 11.0.3 or above; add to core-site.xml: <property><name>hadoop.ssl.enabled.protocols</name><value>TLSv1.2,TLSv1.3</value></property>; do not expect TLS 1.3 to take effect under Java 8.

question: Submitting Spark 3.5 to a Hadoop 2.7 YARN cluster fails with NoSuchMethodError / ClassNotFoundException. What should I do?
context: The official prebuilt Spark distributions are released per major Hadoop version (hadoop-2.7, hadoop-3.2, hadoop-3.3, etc.). The official binaries of the Spark 3.x series mainly target Hadoop 3.2/3.3; running Spark 3.5 directly on a Hadoop 2.7 cluster is not an officially supported combination and often triggers NoSuchMethodError or ClassNotFoundException due to version drift in the Hadoop client libraries.
ground_truth: Download the Spark prebuilt distribution matching the cluster's major Hadoop version (e.g., the hadoop3.3 build), or use the "Hadoop free" package and pull in the cluster's own Hadoop libraries via SPARK_DIST_CLASSPATH=$($HADOOP_HOME/bin/hadoop classpath); confirm HADOOP_CONF_DIR points to the cluster configuration; avoid overwriting the jars of a lower-version Hadoop cluster with the higher-version Spark's jars.

question: After Spark 3.1, yarn.application.classpath is no longer automatically injected into applications, causing Guava/Jackson conflicts. How do I handle this?
context: Since Spark 3.1, the Spark distributions that bundle Hadoop no longer propagate yarn.application.classpath and mapreduce.application.classpath to YARN-submitted applications by default, precisely to prevent failures caused by transitive dependencies pulled from the Hadoop cluster (such as Guava and Jackson) conflicting with Spark's own versions. To restore the old behavior, you can set parameters related to spark.hadoop.hadoopConf.yarn.app.classpath.
ground_truth: Prefer keeping Spark's bundled dependency versions; do not manually put the cluster's guava/jackson jars on --jars. If you truly need to restore the pre-Spark 3.0 propagation behavior, set spark.hadoop.hadoopConf.yarn.application.classpath=<value> per the official migration guide, and repackage/shade your third-party dependencies.

question: A Spark job reports java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: com.google.common.base.Preconditions. How do I troubleshoot this?
context: Guava (com.google.common) is pulled in simultaneously by Hadoop, HBase, spark-core, and other components; the Guava version injected by the cluster usually takes precedence over the application's own version. When the application uses a method from a newer Guava while the cluster ships an older Guava, NoSuchMethodError is thrown at runtime (commonly on classes such as Preconditions, Stopwatch, and Lists).
ground_truth: Use mvn dependency:tree or the Maven Helper plugin to locate the guava version conflict; at packaging time, use maven-shade-plugin to relocate (shade) com.google.common to your own package name, or uniformly exclude transitive guava in your pom and lock it to a version compatible with Spark. Do not use --jars to separately drop in guava to override the cluster classes.

question: At runtime Spark throws an exception about trying to access method com.google.common.base.Stopwatch. How do I resolve it?
context: com.google.guava is packaged inside multiple dependencies such as the HBase client and spark-core; inconsistent Guava versions across different jars cause the wrong version to be class-loaded at runtime, which in turn throws method-access exceptions for Stopwatch and similar methods.
ground_truth: Use the Maven Help plugin (maven-dependency-plugin) to analyze the guava conflict, uniformly lock the guava version and exclude the other transitive versions; alternatively, relocate Guava in the fat jar. Do not bring in another copy of guava via --jars at submission time.

question: At Spark submission, NoSuchMethodError: com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonMappingException.<init>(...) appears. How do I fix it?
context: Spark 3.0+ bundles Jackson 2.10 (different Spark minor versions bundle different jackson-databind versions). When the application or an external SDK (such as the Azure SDK) brings a newer or older jackson-databind to the front of the classpath, jackson-module-scala's call to the JsonMappingException constructor fails with NoSuchMethodError due to the version mismatch.
ground_truth: Uniformize the jackson-databind / jackson-module-scala versions so they match the version bundled with Spark; use the shade plugin to relocate com.fasterxml.jackson; upgrade the conflicting SDK or exclude its transitive jackson in your dependencies to avoid overriding Spark's bundled version.

question: spark-submit reports com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonMappingException.<init>(Closeable,String)V at JacksonModule.setupModule. How do I handle this?
context: The Jackson Scala module (jackson-module-scala) and jackson-databind versions must be strictly matched. After the databind version is downgraded or upgraded, the constructor signature invoked inside JacksonModule.setupModule no longer exists, and NoSuchMethodError is thrown directly.
ground_truth: Downgrade jackson-databind to the version matching Spark's bundled one (for example, from 2.13.5 down to 2.12.x), or upgrade jackson-module-scala to the corresponding version; repackage the fat jar and use dependency:tree to confirm there is ultimately only one jackson-databind.

question: A Spark job reports UnsupportedClassVersionError, warning that the class file version is higher than the current JVM. What should I do?
context: The essence of UnsupportedClassVersionError is a mismatch between the compile-time JDK major version and the runtime JRE major version: a class compiled with a higher JDK (e.g., class file version 61 corresponds to Java 17, and 65 to Java 21) cannot be loaded on a lower-version JVM. Starting with Spark 4.0, at least Java 17 is required; if the running cluster's JDK is low while the program/dependencies were compiled with a higher JDK, this error occurs.
ground_truth: At compile time, use --release 17 (javac/sbt) or configure Maven source/target=17 to align with the running cluster's JDK; upgrade the cluster JRE to the version Spark requires; do not compile with JDK 18+ and then run it on a runtime that only has JDK 17.

question: Spark 4.0 fails to start with UnsupportedClassVersionError, saying Spark requires a higher Java version. Which JDK should I install?
context: Starting from Apache Spark 4.0.0, running requires at least Java 17; meanwhile, the Hadoop cluster's own Java support also changes with version (Hadoop 3.5.0+ officially supports Java 17). To run Spark 4.0 on a YARN cluster whose Hadoop is below 3.5.0, you need to configure a separate JDK for the Spark application that differs from the cluster's.
ground_truth: Upgrade, or explicitly specify JDK 17 separately for the Spark application: do so via spark.driver/executor-related environment variables or a distributed JDK package (--archives); do not let Spark 4.0 run on the cluster's default Java 8/11.

question: PySpark errors with Python in worker has different version 3.7 than that in driver 3.8. How do I resolve it?
context: PySpark requires the Python minor version on the driver and on all executors (workers) to be exactly identical (e.g., all 3.8); when the minor versions differ, PySpark refuses to run directly and reports PYTHON_VERSION_MISMATCH. This commonly happens when container images or cluster nodes have inconsistent Python versions.
ground_truth: Uniformize the Python versions on driver and executors: set export PYSPARK_PYTHON=python3.8 and PYSPARK_DRIVER_PYTHON=python3.8, or in yarn mode specify them via --conf spark.pyspark.python=...; ensure every node/image has the same minor Python version installed.

question: On EMR on YARN, PySpark reports a worker Python 3.7 / driver 3.8 version mismatch. How do I handle it?
context: When the Python version on the EMR container image or nodes differs from the driver side, PySpark validates the minor version during worker startup and throws RuntimeError: Python in worker has different version... as soon as they differ.
ground_truth: At submission, explicitly specify the Python paths on both ends: --conf spark.pyspark.python=/usr/bin/python3.8 --conf spark.pyspark.driver.python=/usr/bin/python3.8; or uniformize the Python version in the base image and rebuild the image.

question: Spark on YARN reports Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits. What should I do?
context: This error means the container's physical/virtual memory exceeded the YARN-configured limit and was killed by the NodeManager. Spark's total executor/driver footprint = heap memory (memory) + memoryOverhead (default max(384MB, 10% of heap)); off-heap memory (Python, native, shuffle, etc.) often pushes the total over the limit.
ground_truth: Gradually raise spark.executor.memoryOverhead / spark.driver.memoryOverhead (up to at most 25% of heap memory); ensure memory+overhead is less than yarn.nodemanager.resource.memory-mb; at the same time, reduce cores per executor and increase the number of partitions; do not set executor memory above 75% of the node's physical memory.

question: A Spark stage fails with exit code 137 / Container killed on request. What is the cause?
context: Exit code 137 (SIGKILL) usually means YARN killed the container after detecting it exceeded memory limits, or the Linux OOM Killer killed the process; when a task repeatedly fails 4 times, the stage is aborted.
ground_truth: Increase executor/driver memory and memoryOverhead; check for data skew making a single task too large; enable off-heap memory management spark.memory.offHeap; confirm the node was not wrongly killed by the OOM Killer (check with dmesg); if necessary, lower spark.executor.cores.

question: After submission, the Spark application stays in Accepted, with required executor memory above max threshold. What is going on?
context: When the configured executor/driver memory plus overhead exceeds the maximum allocatable value per YARN container (yarn.scheduler.maximum-allocation-mb, or the node's yarn.nodemanager.resource.memory-mb), the ResourceManager cannot allocate a container, the application is stuck in Accepted, and the log reports IllegalArgumentException: Required executor memory ... is above the max threshold.
ground_truth: Lower spark.executor.memory / spark.driver.memory / memoryOverhead so they do not exceed yarn.scheduler.maximum-allocation-mb; or on the cluster side, raise maximum-allocation-mb and nodemanager.resource.memory-mb; check whether an overly large PySpark overhead was mistakenly configured.

question: In yarn-client mode, the ApplicationMaster fails to start twice and the log shows it cannot connect to the Driver. What should I do?
context: In yarn-client mode the Driver runs on the client node (often a machine outside the cluster); after the AM starts it needs to connect back to the Driver to register. If the Driver IP is unreachable from the cluster side of the client (firewall, network segment, wrong network interface selected), the AM cannot register and the job fails.
ground_truth: In the client's spark-defaults.conf explicitly set spark.driver.host=<an IP reachable from the cluster>, and use netstat -anp|grep <port> to confirm the sparkDriver port is listening; disable the client firewall and ensure the client and cluster are reachable on the same network segment.

question: Submitting Spark in yarn-cluster mode reports Can't get the Kerberos realm and the AM will not start. How do I troubleshoot?
context: In yarn-cluster mode the Driver starts inside the cluster and loads the client-configured spark.driver.extraJavaOptions; if it contains a client Kerberos config path such as kdc.conf that does not exist on the cluster nodes, the realm information cannot be obtained and the AM fails to start.
ground_truth: Remove the Kerberos-related extraJavaOptions from the driver side, or change it to the real krb5.conf path that exists on the cluster nodes; uniformly deploy krb5.conf inside the cluster and correctly submit secure-cluster jobs via --principal/--keytab.

question: A Spark job reports that org.apache.hadoop.security.authentication.util.KerberosUtil.hasKerberosTicket cannot be found. What is wrong?
context: When the Hadoop version Spark was compiled against by default (e.g., 2.7) differs from the Hadoop version actually pulled into the project / on the cluster (e.g., 2.8.5), method signatures on classes such as KerberosUtil change, and NoSuchMethodError is thrown at runtime.
ground_truth: Make the Hadoop version of the Spark distribution match the cluster's major Hadoop version, or use a Hadoop-free package plus SPARK_DIST_CLASSPATH to pull in the cluster's Hadoop; uniformly align the hadoop-client version in Maven with the cluster.

question: Spark connecting to Hive reports Illegal Hadoop Version: 3.x (expected A.B.* format). What is going on?
context: The shim layer of older Hive (hive-shims-common) parses the Hadoop version number with an old-style regex and cannot recognize the Hadoop 3.x version format, causing shim initialization to fail when Spark integrates Hive. This commonly occurs when pairing a newer Hadoop with an older Hive/Spark combination.
ground_truth: Upgrade Hive to a version that correctly recognizes Hadoop 3.x (e.g., Hive 2.3+/3.1+), or downgrade Hadoop to a range compatible with the paired Hive shim; do not connect Hadoop 3.x to an old Hive Metastore that does not support it.

question: Spark SQL saveAsTable writing to a Hive table throws HiveFileFormat / InsertIntoTableCommand exceptions. What should I do?
context: When the table was created with Hive DDL (a Hive-compatible table), the path Spark takes on a direct saveAsTable write is incompatible with HiveFileFormat, and InsertIntoTableCommand throws directly; merely removing .format() does not fix the root cause.
ground_truth: Before writing, explicitly specify .format("hive") and enable Hive support (SparkSession.enableHiveSupport()); or first create the table with Spark and then write, avoiding mixing the write path with natively Hive-DDL-created tables.

question: SparkSession enableHiveSupport reports Unable to instantiate SparkSession with Hive support. How do I handle this?
context: This error is usually caused by missing hive-exec/hive-metastore-related jars on the classpath, or a missing hive-site.xml, or a Hive version incompatible with Spark's built-in Hive version; Spark only ships built-in support for a specific Hive version.
ground_truth: Confirm that the packaging pulls in the hive dependencies matching the Spark version; place the correct hive-site.xml under conf pointing to the Metastore address; do not mix in multiple copies of hive-exec; if necessary, make the Metastore server-side version match Spark's built-in Hive major version.

question: Spark SQL creating a table / writing data reports Permission denied: user=xxx, access=WRITE, inode="/user/hive/warehouse". How do I resolve it?
context: SparkSQL calls the Hive interface underneath and creates the table directory under hive.metastore.warehouse.dir (default /user/hive/warehouse); when the system user submitting the job lacks read/write/execute permission on that directory, AccessControlException is thrown.
ground_truth: Grant authorization as the hdfs user: hdfs dfs -chmod -R 777 /user/hive/warehouse, or hdfs dfs -chown -R <submitting-user>:hive /user/hive/warehouse; alternatively, prepend export HADOOP_USER_NAME=hdfs to run temporarily as hdfs.

question: Spark writing to HDFS reports Permission denied: user=root, access=WRITE, inode="/". What should I do?
context: After HDFS permission checks are enabled, the job accesses the HDFS root or target path as a local user such as root, and that user has no write permission on HDFS, so RemoteException wraps AccessControlException and throws.
ground_truth: Option one: run export HADOOP_USER_NAME=hdfs before submitting. Option two: sudo -u hdfs hdfs dfs -mkdir -p /path && hdfs dfs -chown -R <submitting-user>:<group> /path. In production, it is recommended to create a dedicated directory in HDFS for the submitting user and grant authorization.

question: When debugging Spark writing to Hive locally/remotely, Permission denied: user=root — root has no permission to write to the cluster HDFS. How to quickly resolve it?
context: When running Spark locally as root, the default user on the HDFS side is also root, and root usually has no write permission on HDFS, which causes writes to the warehouse/output directory to fail.
ground_truth: Before submitting, run export HADOOP_USER_NAME=hdfs to simulate the hdfs user; or in code use System.setProperty("HADOOP_USER_NAME","hdfs"); in formal environments use kinit credentials or grant root authorization on the corresponding HDFS paths.

question: A Spark job reports java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: org/apache/hadoop/fs/FSDataInputStream. What is going on?
context: This is because the runtime environment lacks the Hadoop client libraries. The Spark prebuilt distribution bundles Hadoop client jars; if you downloaded the Hadoop-free version without configuring SPARK_DIST_CLASSPATH, or used a slim image at submission, the Hadoop FileSystem-related classes cannot be found.
ground_truth: Download a prebuilt Spark that bundles the corresponding Hadoop version, or set export SPARK_DIST_CLASSPATH=$($HADOOP_HOME/bin/hadoop classpath); in Docker/images ensure the hadoop-client jar exists and SPARK_DIST_CLASSPATH is correct.

question: Spark 3.3.2 paired with Hadoop 3.3.2 reports org.apache.hadoop.shaded.javax.ws.rs.core.NoContentException at runtime. How do I handle it?
context: Between the hadoop-client-runtime bundled with Spark 3.3.x and the cluster's Hadoop minor version (e.g., 3.3.1 vs 3.3.2), there are differences in the shaded libraries, producing compatibility errors where classes/methods inside the shaded packages cannot be found.
ground_truth: Keep the Hadoop minor version bundled in the Spark distribution as close as possible to the cluster's; or replace hadoop-client-runtime under jars with a version matching the cluster; the safer approach is to use the Hadoop-free package and fully reuse the cluster's Hadoop libraries.

question: A Spark job reports ClassNotFoundException: org.apache.hadoop.fs.s3a.S3AFileSystem. How do I resolve it?
context: Accessing S3A requires the hadoop-aws and aws-sdk-related jars; version mismatches also cause NoClassDefFoundError: software/amazon/awssdk/... or NoSuchMethodError referencing software.amazon/org.apache.hadoop classes, because AWS SDK signatures change heavily across versions and must be recompiled/matched according to the Hadoop version.
ground_truth: Pull in the corresponding versions of hadoop-aws and aws-java-sdk matching the cluster's Hadoop version (e.g., hadoop 3.3.x corresponds to awssdk v2); configure fs.s3a.impl and credentials in core-site.xml; do not mix AWS SDK from different major versions.

question: Submitting Spark on YARN reports the main class cannot be found / the job does not run. How should master be written in the code?
context: If the code hardcodes .master("local[20]") while submission uses --master yarn, the main class / run mode conflict arises and the job is not truly submitted in cluster mode.
ground_truth: Before packaging, comment out .master("local[*]") in the code and let master be decided by spark-submit's --master yarn; uniformly avoid hardcoding master in SparkConf so that switching between local debugging and cluster submission is easy.

question: yarn-client remote submission reports the Driver cannot be reached / cluster ports cannot be reached. How should spark.driver.host be configured?
context: In client mode the Driver is on the client and executors must connect back to it; if the client has multiple network interfaces or uses an elastic IP, Spark may automatically pick an unreachable interface, and executors cannot connect to the Driver.
ground_truth: Add spark.driver.host=<an IP reachable from the cluster> and spark.driver.bindAddress=<the local real IP> to spark-defaults.conf, and set SPARK_LOCAL_HOSTNAME=<elastic IP> in spark-env.sh; confirm the client and cluster are network-reachable and the firewall is open.

question: Local/single-machine Spark reports java.net.BindException: Can't assign requested address: Service 'sparkDriver' failed after 16 retries. What should I do?
context: The Driver RPC port failed to bind, usually because the local hostname resolves to an unreachable address, the port is occupied, or SPARK_LOCAL_IP is not set correctly; Spark retries 16 times by default before giving up.
ground_truth: In spark-env.sh/load-spark-env.sh set export SPARK_LOCAL_IP=127.0.0.1 (or the machine's real IP); in code use config("spark.driver.host","localhost"); when a port is occupied, specify an available port via spark.ui.port/ spark.driver.port or raise spark.port.maxRetries.

question: After upgrading Spark to 3.x, NoClassDefFoundError: scala/Product$class or scala.$minus$minus appears. What is going on?
context: Spark 3 is built on Scala 2.12, while old jars were compiled with Scala 2.11; Scala 2.11 and 2.12 are roughly source-compatible but not binary-compatible, so dropping a 2.11 jar directly onto Spark 3 fails to find the Scala base classes.
ground_truth: Recompile the project with the same Scala version as Spark (Spark 3 → Scala 2.12; Spark 4 → Scala 2.13); ensure all cross-version suffixes such as spark-xxx_2.12 are consistent; do not mix _2.11 dependencies directly into a _2.12 environment.

question: After upgrading to Spark 3, the original Scala 2.11 job reports strange errors. How do I migrate?
context: Scala 2.11 and 2.12 are not binary-compatible; jars compiled against 2.11 cannot run directly on Spark 3 (Scala 2.12), producing class-not-found or symbol-reference errors.
ground_truth: Change the project's scalaVersion to 2.12 and cross-build; verify one by one that all dependencies have a _2.12 version; PySpark projects, being Python wheels, usually run directly, but Scala projects must be recompiled.

question: Code at runtime reports NoSuchMethodError referencing a scala.* class, while the server runs Scala 2.13. What to do?
context: On a Scala 2.13 runtime (such as a new Databricks runtime/Spark 4), dropping in a jar compiled with Scala 2.12 causes NoSuchMethodError due to changed class signatures inside the scala package.
ground_truth: Recompile with scalaVersion := "2.13.x"; ensure every Scala dependency uses the _2.13 cross-version suffix and no _2.12 packages remain.

question: A Spark job reports org.apache.spark.shuffle.FetchFailedException: Connection from ... closed. What should I do?
context: FetchFailed means the reducer failed to fetch the mapper's shuffle blocks; common causes are: the mapper/executor died from OOM, the shuffle service is overloaded, or under a large shuffle the block-fetch concurrency is so high that connections are torn down.
ground_truth: Limit concurrency: --conf spark.reducer.maxReqsInFlight=10 --conf spark.reducer.maxBlocksInFlightPerAddress=10; increase executor/mapper memory; lower the number of partitions or enable the remote shuffle service; appropriately raise spark.shuffle.io.maxRetries.

question: During a large shuffle, Spark reports FetchFailed / block-fetch concurrency too high. How to tune?
context: During shuffle read, the number of concurrent requests per task batch (spark.reducer.maxReqsInFlight) defaults to the maximum integer value, which easily saturates the network/executor under a large shuffle and causes the connection to be closed by the peer.
ground_truth: Set spark.reducer.maxReqsInFlight=10 and spark.reducer.maxBlocksInFlightPerAddress=10 (adjust per cluster); or deploy an external shuffle service so that shuffle data can still be fetched after an executor is lost.

question: Spark reports TimeoutException: waiting for remote fetch of shuffle blocks. How do I handle it?
context: If fetching shuffle blocks exceeds the time set by spark.shuffle.io.connectionTimeout without returning, TimeoutException is thrown; this commonly stems from GC pauses, network congestion, or an overloaded shuffle service.
ground_truth: Raise spark.shuffle.io.connectionTimeout and spark.shuffle.io.maxRetries; increase spark.network.timeout (default =120s, recommended 800s); investigate executor GC and lower the concurrent fetch count.

question: A Spark job reports ExecutorLostFailure / executor heartbeat timed out after 120000 ms. What should I do?
context: An executor that fails to send a heartbeat to the driver within spark.network.timeout (default 120s) is judged lost; common causes are network congestion, long GC pauses, the container being killed by YARN, or preemptible instances being reclaimed.
ground_truth: Raise spark.executor.heartbeatInterval=60s and spark.network.timeout=800s; check whether the executor exited from OOM (exit 137); use non-preemptible instances; investigate node GC pauses.

question: In Spark production, executor timeouts / heartbeat loss happen frequently. How to stabilize?
context: The root cause of heartbeat timeouts is that the executor misses the heartbeat deadline during network congestion or JVM GC pauses; production tuning mainly revolves around enlarging the timeout and heartbeat interval.
ground_truth: In SparkConf set spark.executor.heartbeatInterval=60s and spark.network.timeout=800s; use G1/ZGC to reduce Full GC; monitor executor exit code 137/OOM; if necessary, reduce cores per executor to lower GC pressure.

question: Spark Streaming reading Kafka reports NoClassDefFoundError. How should the kafka-related jars be configured?
context: The spark-streaming-kafka package version must match the cluster's Kafka broker major version; pulling in a spark-sql-kafka/kafka-streaming jar inconsistent with the Kafka version causes runtime class-loading failures.
ground_truth: Use spark-submit --packages to pull in the spark-sql-kafka-0-10 package matching the Kafka version (e.g., kafka 2.8 corresponds to the matching spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.12 version); do not hand-write a jar version that does not correspond to the cluster's Kafka.

question: PySpark writing to Azure reports ClassNotFoundException: org.apache.hadoop.fs.azure.NativeAzureFileSystem. What is going on?
context: Accessing Azure Blob/ADLS requires the hadoop-azure and azure-storage-related jars; when these jars are absent in the image/cluster, the filesystem class cannot be found and NativeAzureFileSystem initialization fails.
ground_truth: Pull in hadoop-azure and the corresponding azure-storage jar per the Hadoop version; configure fs.azure.impl and account credentials in core-site; use a Spark image published by the cloud vendor that ships the cloud-storage connector.

question: The Hadoop-free Spark running on K8s/YARN keeps missing Hadoop classes. How should SPARK_DIST_CLASSPATH be configured?
context: The Hadoop-free (user-provided Hadoop) distribution does not bundle a Hadoop client; the user must assemble the cluster Hadoop classpath into SPARK_DIST_CLASSPATH, otherwise all FileSystem/YARN-related classes are missing.
ground_truth: export SPARK_DIST_CLASSPATH=$($HADOOP_HOME/bin/hadoop classpath); in the K8s case, install the corresponding Hadoop in the executor image's Dockerfile and set the correct SPARK_DIST_CLASSPATH; also configure HADOOP_CONF_DIR correctly.

question: Using old Hive (e.g., 1.2) paired with Spark 2.4+ to connect to the Metastore reports a shims version error. How do I handle it?
context: The old Hive shim layer parses the Hadoop version in A.B.* format and cannot recognize Hadoop 3.x; at the same time, the thrift/metadata versions between Spark and the Hive Metastore must also match, otherwise connection or initialization fails.
ground_truth: Upgrade Hive to 2.3+/3.1 to support Hadoop 3.x; or downgrade Hadoop to the 2.x range compatible with Hive 1.2; confirm hive-site.xml points to the correct Metastore and that Spark's built-in Hive version matches the Metastore major version.

question: After upgrading Spark 4.0, Guava went from 14 to 33 and Jackson from 2.15 to 2.18, and the fat jar reports compatibility errors. How to migrate?
context: The Spark 3→4 upgrade also substantially upgrades underlying dependencies such as Guava and Jackson; the Guava/Jackson APIs shaded or directly referenced in the old fat jar may not exist in the new runtime or may behave differently.
ground_truth: Before migrating, audit the fat jar / shading rules, focusing on the API differences between Guava 14→33 and Jackson 2.15→2.18; upgrade to Scala 2.13 + JDK 17; first temporarily disable ANSI mode, then after upgrading gradually re-enable and fix issues.

question: A Spark job reports a memory error. How much memoryOverhead should be configured for executor/driver?
context: memoryOverhead defaults to max(384MB, spark.executor.memory×0.1), and is used for off-heap (Python, native, shuffle, etc.). Configuring it too small lets the container's total memory exceed the YARN limit and get killed; too large exceeds the node quota.
ground_truth: Gradually raise overhead until it does not exceed 25% of the executor heap memory; ensure (executor.memory + overhead) ≤ yarn.nodemanager.resource.memory-mb and ≤ yarn.scheduler.maximum-allocation-mb; give sufficient overhead for Python/native-heavy jobs.

question: On EMR/cluster, Spark reports Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits. What is the official recommended tuning?
context: This error means the JVM's actual usage (including off-heap) exceeded the allocated memory and the NodeManager killed the container; Spark is especially prone to triggering this due to large off-heap consumption.
ground_truth: In the console/configuration, increase spark.driver.memoryOverhead and spark.executor.memoryOverhead; confirm executor memory does not exceed 75% of the node's physical memory; investigate whether data skew causes a single task's memory to spike.

question: Spark reports java.lang.NoSuchMethodError but the log points to a Hadoop package. Is it a Spark or Hadoop version problem?
context: If the erroring class belongs to a Hadoop package (e.g., org.apache.hadoop.*), it is usually that the cluster Hadoop version differs from Spark's built-in Hadoop, with some methods modified across minor versions; if it is a third-party package, it is mostly a mismatch between Spark's bundled jar and the version pulled in by the application.
ground_truth: Error in a Hadoop package: uniformize the Spark distribution's Hadoop major version with the cluster. Error in a third-party package: use --jars/shade to uniformize versions and avoid conflicts with Spark's bundled ones; use dependency:tree to confirm the final classpath.

question: After upgrading to Spark 3.5.2, commons-io/commons-lang3 were excluded and the job reports class-not-found. What to do?
context: Maintenance releases such as Spark 3.5.2 excluded transitive commons-io/commons-lang3 brought in via commons-compress during dependency governance; if job code directly depends on these trimmed transitive packages, classes may be missing at runtime.
ground_truth: Explicitly declare the required commons-io/commons-lang3 versions in your own project; do not rely on Spark's transitive dependencies; check the dependency changes against the release note and repackage.

question: After PySpark 3.5 upgrades to 4.0, Python 3.8 no longer works. What is the minimum Python version?
context: PySpark raises the minimum required Python version with Spark's major version: starting Spark 4.1, Python 3.9 is dropped, and the Spark 4.0 series has also tightened the supported Python/PyArrow range relative to 3.5; a version too low reports UNSUPPORTED_PACKAGE_VERSION.
ground_truth: Upgrade the runtime environment's Python and PyArrow to match the corresponding Spark version; verify with spark.version and sys.version; at submission, uniformize PYSPARK_PYTHON to a supported minor version.

question: PySpark using a pandas UDF reports package x must be installed / pyarrow version insufficient. What to do?
context: PySpark has minimum version requirements for packages such as pyarrow (the threshold differs across Spark versions, e.g., pyarrow 2.0.0+, 15.0.0+); below the required version it reports UNSUPPORTED_PACKAGE_VERSION.
ground_truth: pip install --upgrade pyarrow (to the version Spark requires); ensure the pyarrow version is consistent across the driver and all executors; when containerized, pin the compatible version in the image.

question: A Spark job reports Task not serializable (NotSerializableException). How do I handle it?
context: The closure captures a non-serializable object (such as a Connection, Executor, or third-party client); Spark fails when it tries to serialize the task closure and send it to the executor.
ground_truth: Change non-serializable objects to be lazily loaded inside the task (create the connection within mapPartitions), or make them transient with custom serialization; distribute large objects that need broadcasting via broadcast, and avoid capturing non-serializable fields in the closure.

question: After FetchFailed, why does Spark not abort the stage directly but go back to the previous stage to recompute?
context: FetchFailed follows a dedicated recovery path: it does not abort the stage after 4 attempts like an ordinary task failure, but immediately goes back to the stage that produced the map output to regenerate the lost data, then reruns the failed task; recurring occurrences indicate shuffle data blocks are persistently being lost.
ground_truth: If FetchFailed recurs, it indicates executors are frequently lost or the shuffle service is abnormal; increase executor memory to prevent OOM, enable the external shuffle service, and raise spark.shuffle.io.maxRetries and the timeout.

question: Starting with Spark 3.5, spark.yarn.max.executor.failures reports deprecated. Which parameter should be used instead?
context: Since Spark 3.5, YARN-specific parameters such as spark.yarn.max.executor.failures and spark.yarn.executor.failuresValidityInterval are deprecated in favor of the unified spark.executor.maxNumFailures / spark.executor.failuresValidityInterval, so as to support resource managers such as YARN and K8s alike.
ground_truth: Change the configuration to spark.executor.maxNumFailures (replacing spark.yarn.max.executor.failures) and spark.executor.failuresValidityInterval; the old parameters are still compatible, but precedence/semantics follow the new migration guide.

question: Initializing the Hive MySQL metastore reports Specified key was too long; max key length is 767 bytes. What should I do?
context: The Hive Metastore uses MySQL as its relational metastore database by default. When the metastore database uses the UTF-8/utf8mb4 character set, MySQL 5.7 and earlier versions have a per-index key length limit of 767 bytes under InnoDB, and certain varchar columns in Hive's CREATE TABLE statements exceed this limit when indexed, so 'Specified key was too long; max key length is 767 bytes' is thrown while automatically creating/validating the metadata tables.
ground_truth: The root cause is that the metastore database's character set makes the index length exceed the limit. Resolution steps: 1) Log in to MySQL and run ALTER DATABASE hive_metastore CHARACTER SET latin1; to switch the Hive metastore database to the latin1 character set; 2) alternatively, run ALTER TABLE ... CONVERT TO CHARACTER SET latin1 on already-created tables; 3) if you insist on utf8, enable innodb_large_prefix and change the row format to DYNAMIC/COMPRESSED (MySQL 5.7.7+ supports 3072-byte indexes by default); 4) after the changes, re-run schematool -dbType mysql -initSchema to initialize the metadata.

question: Which Hadoop version must Hive 3.1.3 be paired with?
context: Each Hive release has a clear Hadoop version compatibility relationship. Per Apache's official release notes, the Hive 3.1.x series is built on Hadoop 3.x, with the official note 'This release works with Hadoop 3.x.y (compatible with some Hadoop 2.x)'; Hive 2.3.x officially states 'This release works with Hadoop 2.x.y' and has not adapted to the RPC and dependency changes of Hadoop 3.x.
ground_truth: 1) Check the release notes for the corresponding version on the Apache Hive download page to confirm the compatible Hadoop major version; 2) a Hive 3.1.x environment should be paired with Hadoop 3.x (e.g., Hadoop 3.3.4); 3) Hive 2.3.x should be paired with Hadoop 2.x (e.g., Hadoop 2.10.x); 4) never run Hive 2.3 directly on Hadoop 3.x, otherwise RPC communication failures or missing dependency classes will occur.

question: Which Spark version should Hive 3.1.2 use when running Hive on Spark?
context: Hive on Spark has a strict Spark version correspondence. The compatibility matrix given in Apache's official Hive on Spark documentation is: Hive master and 3.0.x correspond to Spark 2.3.0; Hive 2.3.x corresponds to Spark 2.0.0; Hive 2.2.x/2.1.x corresponds to Spark 1.6.0. Spark versions outside this range (especially Spark 3.x) have not been officially tested and are prone to missing classes caused by changes in Spark's internal APIs.
ground_truth: 1) Choose the Spark version according to the official matrix: Hive 3.0.x uses Spark 2.3.0, Hive 2.3.x uses Spark 2.0.0; 2) during installation set export SPARK_HOME, and in hive-site.xml configure hive.execution.engine=spark, spark.home and related spark connection parameters; 3) if Spark 3.x must be used, it is recommended to run Spark SQL directly with the Spark engine, or use the Hive Warehouse Connector (HWC), rather than running Hive on Spark directly.

question: Starting Hive reports Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: com.google.common.base.Preconditions.checkArgument. What should I do?
context: Hive and Hadoop each bundle different versions of the Guava library in their respective lib directories. Hive 3.x depends on Guava 19+, while some Hadoop 3.x distributions ship with the older guava-11.0.2.jar or other versions. When Hadoop's older guava is class-loaded before Hive's higher-version guava, calling Preconditions.checkArgument(...), a method only available in the higher version, throws NoSuchMethodError.
ground_truth: 1) Check the guava version in each directory separately: ls $HADOOP_HOME/share/hadoop/common/lib/guava-*.jar and ls $HIVE_HOME/lib/guava-*.jar; 2) compare the version numbers and delete the lower-version jar; 3) copy the higher-version guava (e.g., guava-19.0.jar or newer) into the directory where the other side is missing or has the lower version; 4) after ensuring both sides use the same guava version, restart Hive and re-initialize the metadata.

question: NoSuchMethodError caused by inconsistent guava versions between Hive 3.x and Hadoop — how to handle it?
context: Hive 3.x ships with guava-19.0.jar, while the Hadoop 3.x distribution carries guava-27.0-jre.jar under share/hadoop/common/lib; when Hive's older guava enters the classpath before Hadoop's, the older version lacks method signatures such as com.google.common.base.Preconditions.checkArgument(Z, String, Object), which throws NoSuchMethodError. guava-11.0.2 belongs to the Hadoop 2.6/2.7 era and is not carried by default in Hadoop 3.x.
ground_truth: 1) Check the guava versions under Hadoop's share/hadoop/common/lib and Hive's lib; 2) delete/back up guava-19.0.jar under Hive lib so that it uses guava-27.0-jre.jar from Hadoop common lib; 3) align both sides' guava version to Hadoop's 27.0-jre; 4) restart Hive Metastore and the client to verify that NoSuchMethodError is gone.

question: Hive/Spark-Shell reports ERROR XSDB6: Another instance of Derby may have already booted the database metastore_db. How to resolve?
context: Hive uses the built-in embedded Derby database by default for local metadata. Derby uses the db.lck file in the database directory to prevent two JVMs from booting the same database simultaneously. When the previous Hive/Spark-Shell exited abnormally without releasing the lock, or when multiple processes are started repeatedly in the same directory, the second startup reports ERROR XSDB6: Another instance of Derby may have already booted the database.
ground_truth: 1) First confirm whether there are leftover hive or spark-shell processes holding metastore_db, and kill them with jps or ps; 2) if the lock error persists, delete lock files such as db.lock and db.lck under the metastore_db directory (or delete the entire metastore_db directory directly, noting that this clears the local Derby metadata); 3) for production, it is recommended to use a standalone Metastore such as MySQL/PostgreSQL to avoid Derby's embedded single-process lock issues.

question: Spark-Shell startup reports Caused by: ERROR XSDB6: Another instance of Derby may have already booted /metastore_db
context: When Spark-Shell has Hive support enabled, it creates an embedded Derby metastore database metastore_db in the current working directory. Derby does not allow two JVMs to boot the same database in embedded mode simultaneously; when a previous Spark-Shell/hive process has not closed its connection properly, starting again triggers the XSDB6 double-boot error.
ground_truth: 1) Exit and kill all leftover spark-shell / hive processes; 2) delete metastore_db in the current startup directory (on Windows this is often C:\Windows\System32\metastore_db); 3) alternatively, specify a different startup working directory to avoid reusing the old database; 4) for long-term use, configure an external MySQL metastore connection in spark-defaults.conf to replace the embedded Derby solution.

question: Hive reports Unable to instantiate org.apache.hadoop.hive.ql.metadata.SessionHiveMetaStoreClient. What is the cause?
context: SessionHiveMetaStoreClient failing to instantiate is, at its core, the client being unable to connect to the Hive Metastore service. Common causes include: the Metastore process not being started, a misconfigured metastore URI in hive-site.xml, the external metastore database (MySQL) being unreachable, or the external Metastore database name containing a hyphen that triggers a known Hadoop bug.
ground_truth: 1) Run hive --service metastore to start the Metastore separately and watch its log (default /tmp/<user>/hive.log); 2) check whether hive.metastore.uris in hive-site.xml points to the correct thrift address; 3) verify that MySQL is reachable and that the account, password, and driver are correct; 4) if the external Metastore database name contains a '-' hyphen, rename it using underscores or a hyphen-free name, then recreate the database and re-initialize.

question: The Hive client reports MetaException(message:Could not connect to meta store using any of the URIs provided ... Connection refused)
